entries.title: Sleep and Circadian Rhythm Risks
entries.summary: NASA describes chronic sleep loss, constant work demands, and irregular body-clock schedules as interacting risks to crew health and safety during spaceflight.
excerpts: NASA HRP identifies inadequate sleep and irregular schedules as behavioral performance risks and studies ways to reduce their effects on crew health and safety.
Spaceflight risks can vary by destination and mission profile; use the crew's actual sleep and performance records rather than inferring an individual diagnosis from general research.

entries.title: Spaceflight Cardiovascular and Behavioral Health
entries.summary: NASA HRP tracks cardiorespiratory fitness, behavior, sleep, team function, and other effects of spaceflight hazards; exercise and mission-specific countermeasures help protect crew capability.
excerpts: NASA identifies reduced cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal fitness, behavioral health, teamwork, and sleep as spaceflight risks under continuing research.
NASA-STD-3001 and the flight medical team govern mission-specific health care and countermeasure decisions.

entries.title: Spaceflight Vision and Neuro-Ocular Risk
entries.summary: NASA reports that eye and brain structure can change during spaceflight and studies Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) and its long-term health effects.
excerpts: NASA HRP identifies SANS as a spaceflight risk involving changes to eye and brain structure; visual symptoms should be assessed through mission medical procedures.
The NASA Twins Study included ocular measurements, but those results do not establish individual diagnostic thresholds.

entries.title: Environmental Health and Air Quality
entries.summary: NASA identifies hostile or closed environments as a human-spaceflight hazard involving spacecraft temperature, pressure, lighting, noise, microbes, and immune response.
excerpts: Maintaining a safe spacecraft ecosystem includes monitoring temperature, pressure, lighting, noise, microbes, and immune responses.
Interpret cabin sensor values using the applicable vehicle limits and mission procedures.

entries.title: NASA Spaceflight Hazards
entries.summary: NASA groups human-spaceflight hazards as radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile or closed environments. These hazards can interact.
excerpts: NASA notes that medical care, instructions, and supplies become harder to receive farther from Earth, and that gravity changes affect muscles, bones, the inner ear, and organs.
NASA studies interacting hazards using ground analogs, laboratories, and the International Space Station.

entries.title: NASA Human Spaceflight Risks
entries.summary: NASA HRP connects mission-dependent hazards to risks including immune and vestibular changes, decompression sickness, hypoxia, nutrition, spacewalk injury, reduced fitness, SANS, bone changes, sleep disruption, behavioral health, and radiation-related cancer risk.
excerpts: NASA says risk effects vary for low Earth orbit, lunar, and Mars missions; risks include low oxygen and high carbon dioxide in spacewalk contexts, bone loss in microgravity, sleep disruption, and behavioral effects.
These are NASA research risk categories, not diagnostic cutoffs for an individual astronaut. Follow mission procedures and the flight medical team.

entries.title: NASA-STD-3001 Human Spaceflight Standards
entries.summary: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1 covers crew health and medical care; Volume 2 covers human factors, habitability, and environmental health. Applicability is tailored to each program and mission profile.
excerpts: NASA describes NASA-STD-3001 as a technical standard for minimizing health risks, setting vehicle design parameters, and supporting crew performance.
Mission-specific standards and clinical decisions belong to the program and flight medical team; Dr. SIMI should not invent or replace a standard or prescribe a treatment.

entries.title: The NASA Twins Study: A Multidimensional Analysis of a Year-Long Human Spaceflight
entries.summary: A one-year ISS case study monitored one twin astronaut before, during, and after flight and compared him with his identical twin on Earth. It measured molecular, physiological, ocular, microbiome, and cognitive changes.
excerpts: The study reported changes including body mass, telomere dynamics, genome stability, carotid artery structure, ocular structure, gene expression, metabolism, gut microbiota, and some postflight cognitive measures.

Some averages returned near preflight levels within six months after landing, while other changes persisted. This single-astronaut twin study is contextual evidence, not a universal prediction or personal medical threshold.

entries.title: Monitoring Radiation for Astronaut Health
entries.summary: The Canadian Space Agency describes development of the Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer (CANS), a compact autonomous instrument intended to measure neutron radiation exposure in space continuously.
excerpts: CSA says neutron radiation contributes to about 30% of total radiation on the ISS and describes CANS as a technology under development for continuous autonomous measurement.
The article describes an instrument-development project, not a personal dose limit or a treatment recommendation.
